answer:
FULL SIX-STEP ANALYSIS COMPLETE (executed, see analysis.py / analysis_results.txt).

HYPOTHESIS (data-grounded, testable association — not causal):
"Urban land use is associated with the invasion of introduced plants, but the strength of the association depends on the introduction pathway (and growth form). Plots invaded by Unintentional- and Gardening-pathway species carry significantly more urban land cover than plots without those invaders at every buffer (50, 500 and 1000 m), and — more robustly — plots invaded by these pathway types urbanized more between 1956 and 2009 (increase in urban cover). The Unintentional pathway shows the strongest urban association (largest urban gap, +0.26 at 500 m; strongest urbanization-rate correlation r=+0.42), Gardening is second (r=+0.30), and the AgriForest pathway shows no robust urban association (permutation p>0.1; wide non-significant model CIs). Once habitat type is held constant, static 2009 urban level adds little independent explanatory power, indicating the signal is driven by urban habitat and by urbanization over time rather than by urban cover alone. In growth form, the urban-associated Gardening invaders are predominantly woody/perennial ornamentals (Shrub/tree, Perennial), whereas the most widely invading Unintentional invaders are predominantly annuals. In short: urban land use — and especially urbanization (1956→2009) — is most strongly associated with invasion by unintentionally and horticulturally (gardening) introduced plants, and least with agriculture/forestry introductions."

KEY EVIDENCE
Step 1 (descriptive, urban.2009.500m among pathway-present plots): Gardening 0.284, Unintentional 0.330, AgriForest 0.177. Urban-habitat plots: highest invasion (n.total=2.32) and urban (0.566).

Step 2 (Mann-Whitney + 10k-permutation, invaded vs non-invaded, urban.2009 by buffer):
  Gardening: 50m d=+0.170 p=4.4e-16; 500m d=+0.188 p=3.1e-23; 1000m d=+0.161 p=4.4e-21 (all robust, perm-p=0)
  Unintentional: 50m d=+0.255 p=2.4e-24; 500m d=+0.258 p=7.5e-36; 1000m d=+0.244 p=2.7e-34 (largest, all robust)
  AgriForest: 50m p=0.050/perm 0.143; 500m p=0.0046/perm 0.345; 1000m p=0.013/perm 0.496 (NOT robust — permutation null; n=21)

Step 3 (negative-binomial GLMs, urban.2009.500m, controlling habitat+elevation+distances+cropland):
  n.gard IRR=0.627 [0.23,1.71] p=0.36; n.unint IRR=1.187 [0.49,2.89] p=0.71; n.agfo IRR=0.718 [0.04,13.6] p=0.83 — none significant.
  Combined interaction model (n.total ~ urban × pathway + covars): all interaction terms p=1 (non-significant).
  => static urban level is not an independent predictor once habitat is controlled (collinear with Urban habitat).

Step 4 (urbanization trajectory, urban 1956→2009 delta):
  n.gard: corr(delta)=+0.303 (p=7.3e-15); invaded +0.208 vs non +0.067, MW-p=3.8e-21, perm=0 (robust)
  n.unint: corr(delta)=+0.417 (p=5.7e-28); invaded +0.239 vs non +0.050, MW-p=4.9e-33, perm=0 (robust, strongest)
  n.agfo: corr=+0.047 (ns); perm-p=0.19 (not robust)
  progressive.1956-2009 covariate: not associated (n.gard r=-0.003 ns).
  => the urbanization RATE (delta) is the robust, strongest signal — stronger than static level.

Step 5 (species-level, invasion_success, n=81):
  By pathway, mean number.of.invaded.plots: Unintentional 9.60 (habitat.range 2.77, widest) > Gardening 3.88 (1.95) > AgriForest 2.33 (1.56).
  By growth form: Annual fg 10.58 plots (most invaded) > Perennial fg 4.60 > Shrub/tree 2.96 (tallest, 12.5 m).
  Pathway×growth form: Gardening = Shrub/tree (20) + Perennial (18) = woody/perennial ornamentals; Unintentional = Annual fg (18) = annual weeds; AgriForest = mostly Shrub/tree (6).
  Gardening vs other number.of.invaded.plots: 3.88 vs 7.92, perm-p=0.031 (Gardening less widespread).

Step 6: urban.2009.500m invaded-vs-non gap: Gardening +0.188, Unintentional +0.258, AgriForest +0.048. n.gard r with urban level (2009)=0.286 vs urbanization delta=0.303.

CONCLUSION: urban land use/urbanization is most strongly associated with Unintentional and, secondarily, Gardening pathway invasion (consistent across all spatial scales, stable at 500 m), and the effect tracks urbanization rate (1956→2009 cover increase) more clearly than static urban level once habitat is controlled. AgriForest introductions show no robust urban association.
